categories.label: Reads & consistency
categories.posture: Readers get Always the latest: the newest version as soon as it is published, read from the database while the graph store catches up.
categories.summary: What people see while new data loads, and how far behind a fast view may be.

categories.label: Updates & loading
categories.posture: Each write to the graph store aims at 500 ms and stops at 10 seconds; after it, the worker pauses 25% of the write's time, or 200% while reads wait. A previous copy is kept 15 minutes after a switch or a move.

sections.title: After a switch or a move

categories.summary: How new data is written into the graph store without slowing reads.

categories.label: New-version builds
categories.posture: With New-version builds on, publishes of more than 200,000 changes to graphs set to switch when ready are built in a second copy (copied when there's room, else from the database), 2 at a time per worker, and so are their rebuilds and moves.
categories.summary: Building a graph's next version in a second copy while readers keep the current one.

categories.label: Memory & residency
categories.posture: With Graph residency on, graphs are Standard unless set otherwise. Standard graphs unload after 7 days unread and Coldline after 1 hour; a node unloads graphs from 80% of its memory down to 70%.
categories.summary: Which graphs the graph store keeps in memory, and when it unloads and loads them.

categories.label: Database reads
categories.posture: While a graph is read from the database, each read may run 15 seconds; each process runs 4 reads of one graph at once and 8 in all, and asks the rest to retry.
categories.summary: Limits on reads from the database while the graph store has no version of a graph.

categories.label: Drafts & history
categories.posture: Idle drafts close after 30 days, and closed drafts keep their changes for 30 days. New drafts start public. People may approve their own reviews and may merge them. Each graph may have 10 forks, and a deleted data source can be restored for 30 days.
categories.summary: How long drafts and deleted data last, who sees drafts, and who approves and merges reviews.

categories.label: Imports
categories.posture: Imports match rows by entity id, then URN and the rest the platform knows items by. The replace guard is on: a replace of 1,000 items or more that would delete 50% and make 50% as many again is stopped. An import holds on any refused row.
categories.summary: How imports find existing items, and the guards that stop a mistaken import.

deployment.label: Where reads go, kept for
deployment.means: How long a process may go on sending a graph's reads where it last looked, to its copy or to the database, before looking again. A write tells every process at once, so this only bounds a change that couldn't be announced.

deployment.label: Graphs each worker updates at once
deployment.means: How many graphs each worker updates at once. Builds count among them, so it also caps Builds per worker.

deployment.label: Look for work every
deployment.means: How often a worker looks for graphs to update, besides the nudge each publish sends it.

deployment.label: Most changes in one write
deployment.means: The most changes one write sends; the write target makes writes smaller still.

deployment.label: Longest turn of one graph
deployment.means: A large update stops at a page boundary after this long and carries on in its next turn, so other graphs get theirs.

deployment.label: Written straight after a publish, up to
deployment.means: A change up to this size is written into the graph store straight after its publish; a larger one by the worker. It is also the default of Changes left at the switch.

deployment.label: Longest wait on one write
deployment.means: How long the worker waits on one write to the graph store. A copy waits this plus 15 seconds, 75 by default, and one that takes longer fails that attempt.

deployment.label: A read holds its graph for
deployment.means: How long a person's read keeps its graph from being unloaded.

deployment.label: Database connections per process
deployment.means: Connections each process keeps for versioned graphs. Reads at once per process should stay under it.

deployment.label: Extra connections at a peak
deployment.means: Connections a process may open past its pool at a peak.

deployment.label: Connections for finding where reads go
deployment.means: A small pool of its own that finds where each read goes, so heavy reads can't stop that.

deployment.label: Draft sweep every
deployment.means: How often the worker closes idle drafts and removes closed drafts' changes.

deployment.label: Trash check every
deployment.means: How often the trash is checked for data sources past their restore window.

deployment.label: Most changes a fork reads through
deployment.means: Changes a fork and the graph it came from may have made since they parted before the fork's reads go to the database.

deployment.label: Rows per import step
deployment.means: Rows an import saves to its draft at a time; the early stop decides after the first such step.

deployment.label: Jobs per worker
deployment.means: Import, export and publish jobs each worker runs at once.

deployment.label: Staged rows kept for
deployment.means: Days a finished import's staged rows are kept, to resume or re-run it.

glossary.definition: Where each graph's latest version is held in memory, so reads are fast.
glossary.technical: FalkorDB. Each versioned graph's published main is projected into a key there; Postgres stays the source of truth.

glossary.definition: Where every version of every graph is kept for good. It is the source of truth, so nothing is lost when a graph is unloaded.
glossary.technical: Postgres: the graphver schema, on GRAPHVER_DB_URL or the management database.

glossary.definition: A graph's latest version in the graph store, which readers read.
glossary.technical: A FalkorDB key (projection_state.falkor_graph_name).

glossary.definition: A copy the platform made and manages: it can be unloaded, loaded, moved and built beside.
glossary.technical: owns_falkor_graph is true: a key the platform minted.

glossary.definition: A graph read from a copy its owner keeps in their own graph store. The platform never unloads it, copies it or builds beside it.
glossary.technical: A customer's own FalkorDB key with version control enabled (owns_falkor_graph false), until it is adopted onto a platform key.

glossary.definition: One published state of a graph. Each publish, merge or import makes a new one.
glossary.technical: A commit on main (commit_seq).

glossary.definition: Writing a new version into a graph's copy.
glossary.technical: A projection pass: the projector writes a window of version rows and advances the watermark (projected_commit_seq).

glossary.definition: Bringing a graph that isn't in memory back into the graph store.
glossary.technical: Rehydration: a full seed of a fresh key from Postgres, admitted by the capacity loop (status rehydrating).

glossary.definition: Removing a graph's copy from the graph store to free memory. Nothing is lost: until it is loaded again, it is read from the database.
glossary.technical: Eviction (CacheManager.evict): the key is dropped and the graph marked evicted, with why.

glossary.definition: Building a graph's next version in a second copy while readers keep the current one, then switching.
glossary.technical: A candidate key (projection_state.candidate_*), made by GRAPH.COPY or seeded from Postgres, caught up, checked, then switched to (docs/versioning/04 §5).

glossary.definition: The moment readers move from the current copy to a newly built one, all at once.
glossary.technical: switch_to_candidate: one transaction repins the graph to the build's key; the old key joins retired_keys.

glossary.definition: What readers see while a new version of a graph loads: Always the latest, Keep serving, update in place, or Keep serving, switch when ready.
glossary.technical: build_policy.read_mode_of, applied by service.serving_seq with the mode's lag cap.

glossary.definition: Whether a graph stays in memory when nobody reads it: Always, Standard or Coldline.
glossary.technical: projection_state.residency.

glossary.definition: A residency class: never unloaded.
glossary.technical: residency 'always'; the evictor refuses it.

glossary.definition: A residency class: unloaded after a long time unread, or sooner when memory runs short, and loaded again on its next read.
glossary.technical: residency 'standard'.

glossary.definition: A residency class: unloaded soon after use, and usually read from the database.
glossary.technical: residency 'coldline'.

glossary.definition: One server of the graph store, with its own memory.
glossary.technical: A FalkorDB cluster master, or a standalone or Sentinel-managed instance.

glossary.definition: The share of a node's memory at which graphs start to be unloaded; loads and copies must fit under it.
glossary.technical: high_water_pct of maxmemory.

glossary.definition: The share of a node's memory down to which graphs are unloaded.
glossary.technical: low_water_pct of maxmemory.

glossary.definition: The regular check, every minute by default, of each node's memory, which unloads and loads graphs.
glossary.technical: residency.CapacityLoop.run_once: one leader across workers, under a Postgres advisory lock.

glossary.definition: A background process that updates graphs and runs builds, imports and sweeps.
glossary.technical: The versioning worker (python -m backend.app.services.versioning), by lanes: projection, transfer and bootstrap.

glossary.definition: Counts of lineage between containers, kept ready so large views open fast.
glossary.technical: :AGGREGATED rollup edges, built by the aggregation job and moved by the projector.

glossary.definition: A set of changes to a graph that isn't published yet.
glossary.technical: A branch of kind draft.

glossary.definition: A request to merge a draft, which reviewers approve.
glossary.technical: A merge request.

glossary.definition: A separate copy of a graph to work in, which reads through the original.
glossary.technical: A graph with fork_parent_graph_id and no FalkorDB key of its own (docs/versioning/17).

glossary.definition: Where a deleted data source waits, restorable, before it is removed for good.
glossary.technical: A tombstone (deleted_at); the reaper queues its purge after PURGE_GRACE_DAYS.

glossary.definition: An import that makes the graph, or a view's part of it, match the file: what the file leaves out is deleted.
glossary.technical: reconcileMode=replace.

glossary.definition: What an import's rows find existing items by.
glossary.technical: identifier: entity_id, urn, prop.<name> or prop.<name>,urn.

glossary.definition: A property imports can find items by, kept in an index of its values.
glossary.technical: graphver.entity_keys and key_index (import_export/keys.py).

glossary.definition: The value in force where no level chose one: the deployment's environment variable if it is set and valid, else the built-in value.
glossary.technical: settings_types.Default(code, env, attr).

glossary.definition: A value for the whole platform, chosen by a system administrator.
glossary.technical: scope platform, scope_id ''.

glossary.definition: A value for every graph in one workspace, chosen by its administrators where they may.
glossary.technical: scope workspace, scope_id the workspace id.

glossary.definition: A value for one data source's graph. A fork follows the graph it was forked from.
glossary.technical: scope graph, scope_id the data source id.

glossary.definition: What a system administrator lets workspace administrators choose: the allowed choices, a range, or a lock.
glossary.technical: setting_values.limits on the platform row.

glossary.definition: A value a system administrator set outside the limits. It stays in force, marked as an exception, so tightening a limit never changes a graph without anyone noticing.
glossary.technical: Resolver status exception.

changeWhen: Views of a large graph slow down for a while after each big import: choose Keep serving, update in place for that graph.
Readers must never see part of an update: choose Keep serving, switch when ready, with New-version builds on and memory for a second copy.
The newest data must show the moment it is published, even if slower: keep Always the latest.

effects.down: Update in place: readers can see part of a new version while it is written.
effects.up: Always the latest and Switch when ready: readers see one whole version.

effects.down: Always the latest reads from the database during an update: slower on a large graph.
effects.up: Update in place and Switch when ready keep reads on the graph store at full speed.

effects.down: Switch when ready shows a large change only once it is built.
effects.up: Always the latest and Update in place show a change as it lands.

effects.down: Switch when ready needs room for a second copy while it builds.
effects.up: Always the latest and Update in place need no extra memory.

effects.down: Always the latest sends every read during an update to the database.
effects.up: Update in place and Switch when ready keep reads off the database.

effects.down: Always the latest: under heavy load, a read from the database may be asked to retry.
effects.up: Update in place and Switch when ready serve every read from the graph store.

effects.down: Switch when ready needs spare memory on a graph store node.
effects.up: Always the latest and Update in place cost nothing extra.

guidance.evidence: Measured by the versioning-scale workflow (docs/versioning/09 §2) at 1,000,000 nodes and 1,000,000 edges, a change of 100,000 rows, 4 readers: Always the latest landed in 29 s, reads p99 66 ms, 5% of them from Postgres; update in place 30 s, p99 9 ms, no extra memory; switch when ready by a copy 56 s, p99 9.6 ms, FalkorDB at 2.0x the graph's memory at the peak; by a seed from Postgres 522 s, at 1.1x. No read failed in any mode. With 200 readers at 1M nodes and 2M edges, GRAPH.COPY took 76 to 88 s, past the projector's 75 s socket, three times: the build was dropped and the change written in place. One rule applies the mode to every read: service.serving_seq with build_policy.max_lag_of (0 for latest). candidates.wanted builds beside only above buildAboveRows, on a platform-owned key, with candidateKeysEnabled on; a graph whose summaries live in a graph named from its key, or whose key other data sources read, is written in place (projection._keeps_its_key).
guidance.example: With Always the latest, an import of 100,000 changes shows the moment it is published, read from the database until the graph store has it: slower on a large graph, and without lineage summaries meanwhile.
guidance.means: A publish or an import lands in the database at once, as one new version. Then the graph store, which answers reads fast, is updated, and on a large graph that takes a while. The read mode decides what readers get meanwhile: the newest version, read from the database; the graph store's copy as it is updated; or one whole version until a new copy is built and everyone switches to it.

recommended.why: How reads have always worked: exact, with nothing extra to run. Set Keep serving, update in place on the large graphs whose views must stay fast, and Keep serving, switch when ready only where readers must see one whole version and there is memory for a second copy.

guidance.riskNote: Keep serving, switch when ready needs New-version builds and room for a second copy, or it updates in place. Always the latest reads a graph that is updating from the database, which a busy database feels.

effects.down: Readers get the newest version sooner, from the database when the copy is behind.
effects.up: Readers may see a version further behind the newest one.

effects.down: More reads go to the slower database while the copy catches up.

effects.down: More reads go to the database while a graph catches up.

guidance.evidence: service.serving_seq: behind its head, a key serves main at the version it last published unless committed - held > lag; the lag is build_policy.max_lag_of(mode): 0 for latest, else GRAPHVER_READ_MAX_LAG (-1, any). The same bound decides whether a rebuild or a move can be built beside the key (service._beside_ok).
guidance.example: A graph set to update in place keeps serving its copy, however many versions it falls behind, until it catches up.
guidance.means: With Keep serving, update in place or Keep serving, switch when ready, readers stay on the graph store's copy while it catches up, at the version it last finished. This caps how many versions behind that may be. Further behind, readers go to the database for the newest version until the copy catches up. Always the latest doesn't use it: it never serves an older version.

recommended.why: The copy catches up on its own, and until it does readers keep a whole recent version at full speed. A limit sends them to the database instead, which is slower on a large graph.

guidance.riskNote: A small limit sends readers of a busy graph to the database whenever it falls that far behind, which is slower and loads the database.
guidance.summary: How many versions behind the newest one a graph's copy may still serve readers while it catches up.

effects.down: Reads wait less behind each write.
effects.up: Reads on the node can wait longer behind each write.

effects.down: More, smaller writes: a large update takes longer.
effects.up: Fewer, larger writes: a graph updates sooner.

guidance.evidence: projection._laddered: a chunk slower than statementTargetMs halves the next, no narrower than 50 rows for being slow (_SLOW_FLOOR). A write holds the graph's write lock, and every read of it on that node, while it runs (docs/versioning/04 §5, Serving while it updates).
guidance.example: Each write to the graph store aims to take about 500 ms. One that runs longer makes the next one smaller, so a read waits about that long at most behind a write.
guidance.means: While the worker writes new data into a graph's copy, every read of that graph on the same node waits for the write to finish. So writes are kept short: one that takes longer than this makes the next one smaller, down to 50 changes.

recommended.why: Short enough that a read waits about half a second at most behind a write, long enough that writes aren't split into tiny pieces.

guidance.riskNote: Too low splits writes into many small ones and slows large updates; too high makes reads wait behind long writes.
guidance.summary: How long each write to the graph store aims to take, so reads on the same node keep their turn.
symptoms: Canvases stall while a graph updates
Updates take too long to land

takesEffect.text: The next write, once the worker reads its settings again, which it does as it updates each graph.

changeWhen: Reads freeze for several seconds during big updates: lower it.
Updates of a large graph keep failing on timeouts: raise it a little.

effects.down: No read waits long behind a write.
effects.up: A read can wait longer behind one write.

effects.down: More writes are stopped and redone in halves: a heavy update takes longer.
effects.up: Fewer writes are stopped and redone: a heavy update lands sooner.

guidance.evidence: projection._laddered: every chunked write's budget is min(the client's write budget, writeCeilingSecs), on every FalkorDB mode; a timeout halves the chunk and sends the halves again, down to one row, then retries it 3 times (GRAPHVER_PROJECTION_FLOOR_RETRIES). FalkorDB rolls back a statement it aborts, and every projector write is an idempotent MERGE, SET or DELETE.
guidance.example: A write still running after 10 seconds is stopped and sent again in halves; reads behind it wait no longer than that.
guidance.means: A write still running after this long is stopped and sent again in halves, so no read waits longer than this behind one write. The graph store undoes a stopped write, so nothing is left half-written.

recommended.why: Long enough for any well-sized write, short enough that a stuck write never holds a node's reads for long.

guidance.riskNote: Set very low, writes that can't fit are halved down to one change and retried, and an update can fail.
guidance.summary: The longest one write to the graph store may run before it is stopped and split.
symptoms: Reads freeze during big updates
Updates fail with timeouts on a large graph

takesEffect.text: The next write, once the worker reads its settings again, which it does as it updates each graph.

changeWhen: Canvases are slow whenever a graph updates: raise it.
Updates take too long while reads are quiet: lower it.

effects.down: Reads get less of the node's time while a graph updates.
effects.up: Reads get more of the node's time while a graph updates.

effects.down: Updates land sooner.
effects.up: Updates take longer to land.

guidance.evidence: projection._pace: after each write a pause of pacingRatio times its time, readPressureRatio times while the web tier marks reads on the node as starving (agg:readpressure:<node>), at most 5 s (_PACE_MAX_S), none under 5 ms.
guidance.example: A write that takes 500 ms is followed by a 125 ms pause, so reads on that node get about 20% of its time while a graph updates.
guidance.means: After each write the worker pauses, so reads waiting on that node go first. At 0.25 it pauses a quarter as long as the write took, at most 5 seconds; at 0 it pauses only while reads are waiting (Pause while reads wait).

recommended.why: Reads get a fifth of the node's time even while a graph updates, and updates still land quickly. While reads are waiting, the pause grows anyway (Pause while reads wait).

guidance.riskNote: High values slow every update; 0 lets a long update hold the node's reads.
guidance.summary: The pause after each write to the graph store, as a share of the time it took.

changeWhen: Reads time out or are asked to retry while a large graph updates: raise it.
Updates stall during busy hours: lower it.

effects.down: Waiting reads stay queued longer.
effects.up: Waiting reads catch up faster during an update.

effects.down: More reads may time out under load while a graph updates.
effects.up: Fewer reads time out under load while a graph updates.

effects.down: An update keeps its pace while reads are busy.
effects.up: An update slows more while reads are busy.

guidance.evidence: projection._pace: readPressureRatio replaces pacingRatio while reads on the node are starving and it is the larger, at most 5 s; graphver_projection_yields_total counts each such pause.
guidance.example: While reads on a node are waiting, a write that takes 500 ms is followed by a 1,000 ms pause: reads get about 67% of the node's time until they catch up.
guidance.means: When reads on a node are queueing, the worker pauses this share of each write's time instead, at most 5 seconds, so readers catch up. It applies only when it is longer than the usual pause.

recommended.why: While reads wait, each write is followed by a pause twice as long, so reads get two thirds of the node's time until they catch up.

guidance.riskNote: High values can hold an update back for as long as reads stay busy.
guidance.summary: The longer pause after each write while reads on the node are waiting.

changeWhen: Graph store memory stays high for a while after each switch or move: lower it.
Long-running reads fail just after a switch: raise it.

effects.down: Memory is freed sooner after a switch.
effects.up: Old copies hold memory longer after each switch.

effects.down: A read that started before a switch is likelier to fail when its copy is removed.
effects.up: Long reads under way at a switch always finish.

guidance.evidence: Stamped on retired_keys when a build switches (switch_to_candidate) or a key is moved: retireAfter = now + retireGraceSecs; the retire loop drops a due key once the new one has caught up. Its range starts at 660 s, past versioned_sources.CACHE_TTL_SECS (600 s), within which a newly versioned data source may still read its own key.
guidance.example: After a switch or a move, the previous copy stays 15 minutes; then it is removed and its memory freed.
guidance.means: When readers move to a new copy, after a new-version build or a move, the old copy stays in the graph store this long, so reads already running finish on it. Then it is removed and its memory freed. It is at least 11 minutes.

recommended.why: Fifteen minutes is far longer than any read, and the memory comes back soon after.

guidance.riskNote: Long values keep two copies of a graph in memory after every switch; the graph store needs room for both.
guidance.summary: How long a graph's previous copy is kept after a switch or a move, so reads under way finish on it.
symptoms: Graph store memory stays high after a switch
